claims.text: The cast refractory multi-principal element alloy has limited ductility.
The cast refractory multi-principal element alloy has a coarse-grained structure.
Refractory multi-principal element alloys may form undesired intermetallic phases following compositional modification.
Minor additions of Mo and Re can produce a negative lattice misfit.
Minor additions of Mo and Re provide solid-solution strengthening.
Negative lattice misfit promotes N-type rafting of gamma-prime precipitates.
Severe plastic deformation at an optimized strain rate will refine the target alloy to grain sizes below 50 nm.
Mo/Re addition followed by severe plastic deformation will stabilize a dual FCC/BCC solid-solution structure.
Gamma-prime precipitates produced by negative-misfit rafting will pin boundaries and stabilize grain sizes below 50 nm.
A high density of high-angle grain boundaries will be stabilized by solute drag.
The negative lattice misfit will suppress nucleation of brittle Laves or Heusler intermetallic phases.
Processing at approximately 1800 rpm or higher can cause a bimodal grain-size distribution.
High rotational speed can substantially reduce the high-angle grain-boundary fraction.
Above a temperature-dependent stability limit, diffusion and surface-energy effects can overcome entropy stabilization and cause phase separation.
Grain refinement will substantially increase the yield strength of the proposed refractory alloy.
Mechanical milling and grain refinement will increase hardness.
The processed alloy will retain greater ductility than the as-cast alloy while gaining strength.
The final nanocrystalline FCC/BCC microstructure will contain no brittle intermetallic phases.

contradictions.description: The target phase constitution is described as a dual FCC/BCC solid solution, but the proposed mediator and mechanism require a gamma/gamma-prime matrix–precipitate structure and N-type rafting. Gamma-prime is an ordered precipitate phase, not the proposed BCC solid-solution phase, so the operative phase constitution is internally inconsistent.

The mechanism relies on gamma-prime precipitates as grain-boundary pinning points, whereas the outcome is framed as an FCC/BCC solid-solution microstructure without additional intermetallic phases. The hypothesis does not explain whether gamma-prime remains present, transforms into BCC, or is excluded from the claimed final phase constitution.
